assessment:
The table counts eight tutors and assumes you can find anything. Play like that is false, because it is. This library holds one card the deck cannot replace and almost no answers at all, so a wish here is a decision about which hole you are filling, not a blank cheque.

The scarce half is the counter SOURCE. Sacrifice outlets are everywhere — eight of them cost no mana — and exactly one of those also places a -1/-1 counter. That is Yawgmoth, Thran Physician, and he is the default wish in nearly every entry below. Fire the first tutor at that hole and stop hunting for something cleverer.

Kill one habit before you start. Do not send a tutor after an altar to loop with Mikaeus. Stack 001 checked all five — Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Viscera Seer, Carrion Feeder, Blasting Station — and each one gives you exactly one undying return and stops. With Mikaeus out, an altar activation is worth one extra death. Sequence it as one and never as a kill.

The line that actually loops is Mikaeus plus Devoted Druid, and here is the figure that should change how you play: you assemble it in one game in forty on your own, and roughly one game in three once a tutor is counted. So do not treat the tutor as a shortcut to that kill. The tutor IS that kill — when one half is on the board, spend the wish on the other half and stop waiting for a draw step to do it for you.

Trust the depth and stop hoarding. You see a tutor in more than three quarters of your games, at a mean of turn 2.7, so cast the first one at the first hole instead of saving it for a clever turn that may never arrive.

Name the card knowing its delivery speed. Demonic Tutor, Diabolic Intent, Grim Tutor and Survival of the Fittest hand you the card now. Vampiric Tutor, Imperial Seal and Worldly Tutor put it on TOP — those are appointments, not arrivals — so fire the two instants at the end step before your untap and cut the transit to nothing. Green Sun's Zenith is the only one that puts a body straight onto the battlefield, and it shuffles itself back in, so spend it early without agonising.

One standing order for every entry below. Nothing here fetches on the promise of the Blowfly kill, because no checker has signed that line. Go and get Blowfly Infestation when the grind wants another counter source. Never go and get it as a two-card win.

tutors.notes: Two mana, any card, no strings — and the only kind of wish here that can name a land. Point it at the hole and cast it; this is not the tutor you save.

targets.scenario: Turn 3. Hapatra came down on turn 2 as she does in almost every game, a Snake or two beside her, and nothing in hand places a counter more than once.
targets.why: Take the default wish and take it now. Of the eight sacrifice outlets in this deck that cost no mana, he is the only one that also places a counter — that single asymmetry is the whole deck, and every activation of his is a card, a ping and a Snake. Never aim that counter at the creature you are sacrificing; stack 001 settled it as the ability's only target, so it goes illegal on resolution and you lose the counter and the draw together. Aim somewhere else, or choose no target at all and just take the card.

citations.quote: k tutors plus the card act like k+1 copies of *every* card.
Payoffs without the enabler are blanks until the engine exists

targets.scenario: Mikaeus, the Unhallowed is already on the battlefield and you have four mana untapped.
targets.why: Fetch and cast in the same turn — two for the tutor, two for the Druid — so the loop is live before anyone gets a turn to answer the half you just showed them. Stack 001 signed this one: infinite deaths, placements, Snakes and drain, and explicitly not mana. It needs no haste, because the untap cost carries no tap symbol. Take the three green off the first pass, then run it as bodies and drain rather than as ramp.

targets.scenario: You are behind. Two wide boards across the table, your engine half-built, and real damage arriving next rotation.
targets.why: Fetch the rebuild, not the reset. Counters on each creature trigger Hapatra once per creature, fill Nest of Scarabs, and hand Necroskitter every opposing creature that dies carrying one — you come out of your own sweeper wider than you went in. Your 1/1s die too and you should be delighted, because you already banked the triggers. Take Toxic Deluge instead only when you need the board gone regardless of value: it places nothing and pays you nothing.

targets.scenario: A reanimator or graveyard seat is the actual problem — recursion every turn cycle, and killing the body has stopped meaning anything.
targets.why: Go and get a land, and do not feel strange about it. Your interaction answers creatures and nothing else, this is the one card in the 99 that touches a graveyard, and an unrestricted wish is the only thing that can name it. Budget the whole cost before you commit: the land, three mana and the land itself going to exile. Fire it before you need Phyrexian Reclamation or Eternal Witness, because it empties your yard along with theirs.

tutors.notes: The sacrifice is a cost, not a drawback — with a drain converter out you get paid to tutor. Run the death through your payoffs before you cast it, not after.

targets.scenario: Turn 3, Hapatra out, a spare Snake standing around, and Blood Artist or Grim Haruspex already on the battlefield.
targets.why: Same wish as Demonic Tutor at effectively no cost. Feed it a token whose death already pays you and take the one enabler the deck cannot replace. Check the order first — Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat, Blood Artist and Morbid Opportunist all want to be on the battlefield before that Snake dies, so deploy them and tutor second.

targets.scenario: Devoted Druid has survived a turn on the battlefield, you are one land drop from six mana, and the table's creature removal has been counted and spent elsewhere.
targets.why: Fetch him the turn BEFORE you can cast him. He costs six and you only reach six mana around turn six, so trying to tutor and cast in one turn is how the attempt slips a full rotation and hands three players a draw step to find an answer. Present the second half only once you have counted open mana at every seat.

citations.quote: assume every held answer appears the moment you present lethal, and count the table's open mana before committing

targets.scenario: A control seat has held up four or more mana for two turns — assume the sweeper — and your board is wide.
targets.why: Fetch the converter that survives the wrath. It drains each opponent whenever a creature you control dies, so their sweeper becomes your table-wide hit, and an enchantment sits out of range of every creature removal spell they are holding. Zulaport Cutthroat does the same job on a body that dies to that same wrath — take Bastion when the sweeper is the read.

tutors.notes: It shuffles itself back in, so spending it at X=1 on turn 1 costs you nothing you cannot find again. It is also the only wish that puts a body onto the battlefield, which is why the enter trigger matters here and nowhere else. Know its ceiling: green creatures only, so it can never name Yawgmoth, Mikaeus or Walking Ballista, and it is never your closing wish.

targets.scenario: Turn 1, one green source, an otherwise ordinary hand.
targets.why: Cast it for one and buy a bigger turn 2. Hapatra lands on turn 2 in nearly every game regardless; this is how she lands with company instead of alone, and it turns your turn 3 into a four-mana turn. Take Birds of Paradise instead when your black sources are the thin half of the hand.

targets.scenario: Mikaeus, the Unhallowed is on the battlefield and you have three mana available.
targets.why: This is the best card Zenith casts in this deck. It puts the verified other half straight onto the battlefield at X=2, so there is never a turn where you sit holding the Druid and telegraphing the kill. Take the three green from the first pass and then play the loop as deaths, Snakes and drain — stack 001 is explicit that it is not a mana loop.

targets.scenario: A repeatable counter source is already running and the board needs to become a clock.
targets.why: Buy the drain that triggers on placement rather than on death, because placement is where your engine is loud — it hits every opponent every time a counter goes anywhere. Most tables forget Zenith reaches X=3, and nobody points removal at a Spider until it is far too late.

targets.scenario: Your sweeper or your best tutor is in the graveyard, the game has gone long, and you have four mana.
targets.why: Zenith puts her onto the battlefield, so the enter trigger happens immediately — that is the whole difference between this tutor and Worldly Tutor, which would only put her on top of your library. Buy back Demonic Tutor or Black Sun's Zenith and collect a sacrifice body in the same card.

tutors.notes: Three mana and three life for a card you could have had for two. Cast it when the hole is genuinely the enabler, and remember this deck already bills you through Yawgmoth, Bitterblossom, Phyrexian Reclamation, The One Ring and three painlands.

targets.scenario: Turn 3 or 4, no repeatable counter source in hand, and the cheaper tutors are spent or absent.
targets.why: Pay the three life for the enabler and never for a luxury. You are buying the one card the census says has no replacement, and that is the only purchase worth this price. If the hand already contains a counter source, hold this and cast a body instead.

targets.scenario: The engine is running, bodies are flowing, and your hand is empty while you top-deck.
targets.why: Fetch the card that turns your board back into a grip. Every Snake, Insect, Faerie and Elf Warrior is a 1/1, so equipping is pay one, draw two, over and over. When the board is ahead of the hand, take the engine over any single spell you could name instead.

targets.scenario: The game is long, your mana is untapped, and the cards left in your hand are creatures you no longer need.
targets.why: Spend one wish to buy a repeatable one. This is the single time paying three mana and three life for a two-mana enchantment is right: you are not buying a card, you are buying every remaining tutor the game will ask you for, and your dead creature cards become the fuel.

citations.quote: k tutors plus the card act like k+1 copies of *every* card.

tutors.notes: Sorcery speed, and the wish arrives on your next draw. That makes it an early-game card and a scheduling tool — cast it before the game has a shape, never at the pivot, or you announce the pivot a full turn in advance.

targets.scenario: Turn 2, board empty, and nothing in hand places counters more than once.
targets.why: Schedule the enabler. Cast the Seal on turn 2, hold him on turn 3, deploy him on turn 4 on curve, for two life you will not feel that early. Do this and the Seal costs you a draw step nobody was watching; do it on turn 6 and it costs you the surprise.

targets.scenario: Turn 4 or 5, Devoted Druid or Walking Ballista already on the board, and the game is plainly going long.
targets.why: Let the Seal's slowness be free. He costs six and you reach roughly six mana on turn six, so name him a turn early and the transit costs you nothing you were going to spend. Then hold him until the table's answers are counted rather than casting him the moment the mana exists.

citations.quote: assume every held answer appears the moment you present lethal, and count the table's open mana before committing

targets.scenario: Turn 1 on the play, a Swamp down, and a hand that already contains a counter source.
targets.why: The odd one: name the enchantment nobody expects a tutor to find. A body every upkeep for one life feeds Skullclamp, feeds every sacrifice outlet, pays Diabolic Intent's cost forever and makes your first four turns cheap to survive. Take it only when the enabler is already handled — the source outranks the fodder every single time.

tutors.notes: The most powerful card in this section, because it is the only wish you get more than once — and it reveals. After the second activation the table knows exactly what you are assembling, so spend your protection or your politics from that moment, not after the third.

targets.scenario: Any turn with a green source open and a creature card in hand you no longer need — a spent mana dork, a redundant body.
targets.why: Activate on the first turn you can and take the census answer every time. The discard barely registers here: Phyrexian Reclamation buys a creature back for two mana and two life, and Eternal Witness buys the card back with a body attached. Do not save the activation for a better idea — you get another one next turn.

citations.quote: Payoffs without the enabler are blanks until the engine exists

targets.scenario: Late game, six mana in sight, and the table's creature removal has been counted and already spent.
targets.why: Assemble across two activations instead of praying for a draw: Mikaeus now, Walking Ballista next turn. Stack 001 verified that package with any free outlet as genuinely unbounded, and it needs three cards rather than two because the anthem keeps a counterless Ballista alive — the outlet does the recycling the Ballista cannot do for itself. You own eight free outlets, so that third piece is the one you never have to look for.

targets.scenario: A creature deck is going wide across the table and Black Sun's Zenith is already in your hand.
targets.why: Turn their board into yours. Every creature an opponent controls that dies with a -1/-1 counter on it comes back under your control, and your sweeper puts a counter on every creature at once. Cast the Zenith for exactly enough — X of one collects every 1/1 they have and costs you the least of your own board.

targets.scenario: A blue seat is untapped with a wheel or a big draw spell, and you have one green open plus a creature card you can bear to lose.
targets.why: Activate on their turn and answer the problem after it starts — no other tutor in this deck can do that. Survival puts the card in your hand immediately and Bowmasters has flash, so the extra draws cost them life and hand you an Army to sacrifice. Hold the green up whenever a draw seat is untapped and you have fodder to spare.

tutors.notes: Instant speed, two life, and it costs you your draw step. Fire it at the end step before your untap so the card is on top for your draw and nobody gets a turn to act on what you just told them.

targets.scenario: The end step of the opponent before you, turn 2 or 3, engine incomplete.
targets.why: Fire it at the last legal moment and the wish is yours before anyone can respond to the information — zero turns in transit, which is the entire card. Spend it on the turn the answer matters and never on curiosity, because you are paying a draw step for it.

citations.quote: prefer committing at the end step before your own turn so the table's chances to respond are spent

targets.scenario: The aggro seat is lethal-adjacent to somebody, your blockers do not stop it, and rebuilding will not be enough.
targets.why: Reach for the panic button and sequence it as one. Deluge places no counters, so Hapatra, Nest of Scarabs and Necroskitter give you nothing — cast it for the board, not for value, and pay the life out of a total this deck spends freely anyway. Tutor at their end step so it is in hand for your main phase.

citations.quote: spending removal on sight instead of at the last profitable moment

targets.scenario: Mikaeus is on the battlefield with any free sacrifice outlet, and you can spare two mana next turn.
targets.why: Name the third card and win. Stack 001 verified this one as genuinely unbounded and it needs no drain payoff at all: cast the Ballista with a counter, remove it for a damage, sacrifice the 1/1 to the outlet, undying returns it with a counter, remove that one, repeat. It needs the outlet precisely because Mikaeus's anthem keeps a counterless Ballista alive — it never gets to kill itself.

targets.scenario: Turn 5 or later, four mana you can hold up, and one opponent's commander is the reason your creatures keep dying.
targets.why: Name a land and hold a trick nobody at this table is playing around. You can put it onto the battlefield from your hand for four at instant speed, no land drop required, and its arrival phases out a creature — theirs, to blank an attacker, or yours, to walk Yawgmoth out from under a wrath or a targeted kill. Buy the turn and know what you bought: it comes back on its controller's untap step, so this is a tempo answer, not a removal spell. It is the closest thing to a counterspell this library contains.

citations.quote: Except for rules and effects that specifically mention phased-out permanents, a phased-out permanent is treated as though it does not exist.
Simultaneously, all phased-out permanents that had phased out under that player’s control “phase in.”

tutors.notes: One green mana at instant speed, and the reveal is public. Fire it on the end step before your untap so the card is in hand on your turn and the table has no window to act on what it just saw.

targets.scenario: Turn 2 or 3, one green open at the end of the turn before yours, no counter source in hand.
targets.why: Cheapest possible route to the card that matters, so take it and plan for the consequence. The reveal tells three players he is coming: hold a second body, keep Heroic Intervention up if you have it, and do not tap out on the turn he lands.

citations.quote: prefer committing at the end step before your own turn so the table's chances to respond are spent

targets.scenario: Mikaeus resolved this turn and survived, and you untap into three mana.
targets.why: Name the other half of the only verified two-card loop in the deck. Draw it, cast it, and go on the same turn — it needs no haste, because the untap cost carries no tap symbol, which is exactly what makes this reveal worth the telegraph.

targets.scenario: No engine yet, and the problem is a single small body — a mana dork, an Orcish Bowmasters, an opposing enabler.
targets.why: Take the removal that is also a combo piece: it costs exactly the mana you can spare, kills the thing now, and stays on the board as the third piece of the Mikaeus kill later. Do not expect a Snake out of it — it deals damage rather than placing counters, so Hapatra sits this one out.

gaps: Every default wish in this book is the same card, and a table that watches you fetch Yawgmoth once will kill him on sight. Decide your second wish before the first one resolves: Devoted Druid under Mikaeus is the verified backup engine, and Phyrexian Reclamation buys Yawgmoth back for two mana and two life.

Three of these eight deliver to the top of your library, so the wish can be answered before it ever arrives. Fire Vampiric Tutor and Worldly Tutor at the end step before your untap, and treat Imperial Seal as an early-game card only.

No tutor here can find an artifact or an enchantment answer, because the library holds none — your interaction covers one class of five and it is creatures. The only breadth on this whole fetch list is two lands: Abstergo Entertainment against a graveyard, Talon Gates of Madara against one creature. Against a resolved prison piece the tutors are blank, so race it or politick it, and say which on turn one.

Do not spend a wish on an altar to loop with Mikaeus. Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Viscera Seer, Carrion Feeder and Blasting Station each give exactly one undying return with him out — stack 001 checked all five. Sacrificing to a free altar under Mikaeus is one extra death of value, and it should be sequenced as one.

Nothing in this section fetches on the promise of the Blowfly kill, the Ivy Lane pairings or Scurry Oak, because no checker has signed those lines. Go and get Blowfly Infestation when the grind wants another counter source, take the kill if the table hands it to you, and never build a turn around it.
Green Sun's Zenith cannot name Yawgmoth, Mikaeus or Walking Ballista — green creatures only. It is your tempo tutor and your cheapest one, and it is never the wish you close with.
